presentingComplaint: Six weeks of persistent cough with recent blood-streaked sputum and unintentional weight loss.
history: 68-year-old man, 45 pack-year smoker (still smoking 10/day), presents with a chronic cough that has changed in character over the past 6 weeks, now with intermittent blood-streaking of sputum on several occasions. Reports 7 kg unintentional weight loss over 3 months, reduced appetite, and progressive exertional breathlessness. Denies fever, rigors, night sweats or contact with tuberculosis. Occasional dull right-sided chest ache. Past history: COPD (mild), hypertension. No prior malignancy. No recent travel.
examination: Cachectic, clubbing of the fingers. Right upper-zone reduced air entry with focal coarse crepitations; no signs of consolidation with bronchial breathing. No stridor, no facial/neck swelling, no palpable supraclavicular nodes on this visit. No pallor, no jaundice. Afebrile and not toxic-appearing. Chest wall non-tender.
imaging: Chest X-ray: 4 cm speculated right upper-lobe mass with hilar prominence, no cavitation, no effusion. Contrast CT thorax/upper abdomen: 4.2 cm spiculated RUL mass with ipsilateral hilar and mediastinal (station 4R/7) lymphadenopathy; no distant metastasis on this study; adrenals normal.
microbiology: Sputum for AFB smear x3 negative; routine sputum culture negative. (Performed to exclude TB/infection.)
finalDiagnosis: Lung cancer (non-small-cell, right upper lobe primary with mediastinal nodal involvement)
citations: ACCP/CHEST Diagnosis and Management of Lung Cancer (Evidence-Based Guidelines, 3rd ed) 2013
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective. Empiric antibiotics are not indicated; AFB/culture were sent to exclude TB and post-obstructive infection, both negative.
contraindications: No antibiotic indicated; avoid reflexive empiric therapy for a non-resolving mass without infective evidence
Contrast CT: verify renal function/eGFR before iodinated contrast
Biopsy: check platelets/coagulation and stop antiplatelets/anticoagulants beforehand
edgeCases: Cough with haemoptysis and weight loss in a heavy smoker mimics reactivating pulmonary TB - always send AFB and do not anchor
Mild hyponatraemia (SIADH) and hypercalcaemia can be paraneoplastic clues to small-cell vs squamous histology
A non-resolving 'pneumonia' or persistent focal opacity in a smoker warrants CT and tissue diagnosis, not repeat antibiotic courses
expectedMaiK: In a heavy smoker over 50 with a new spiculated lung mass, chronic cough, haemoptysis and unexplained weight loss, lung cancer is the leading diagnosis; pursue staging CT and tissue biopsy rather than empiric antibiotics, while excluding TB given the overlapping picture.
